headings.title: Introduction and Definition of Hypertension
headings.content: Hypertension, commonly referred to as high blood pressure, is a chronic medical condition in which the systemic arterial blood pressure is persistently elevated. For nursing students in Nigeria, understanding hypertension is vital as it constitutes a major burden in both primary and tertiary healthcare settings. Blood pressure is measured in millimeters of mercury (mmHg) and is recorded as two numbers: systolic pressure, representing the pressure in the arteries when the heart beats, and diastolic pressure, representing the pressure in the arteries when the heart rests between beats. A single elevated reading is not sufficient to diagnose hypertension; rather, diagnosis requires multiple elevated readings taken on separate occasions by a qualified healthcare professional. Chronic hypertension places excessive mechanical stress on the arterial walls, leading to microvascular and macrovascular damage throughout the body. Left untreated, it significantly increases the morbidity and mortality associated with cardiovascular diseases, cerebrovascular accidents, and renal failure. As front-line healthcare providers, nurses play a critical role in the early identification, monitoring, and ongoing education of individuals with or at risk for hypertension. Recognizing the asymptomatic nature of the condition in its early stages underscores the importance of routine blood pressure screening during every patient contact in Nigerian hospitals and community clinics.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Normal Blood Pressure Ranges
headings.content: The pathophysiology of primary (essential) hypertension is multifactorial and involves complex interactions between genetic, environmental, and physiological mechanisms. Key systems involved include the sympathetic nervous system, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), and renal mechanisms regulating sodium and water balance. Overactivity of the sympathetic nervous system increases heart rate and cardiac output, while vasoconstriction raises systemic vascular resistance. Similarly, an overactive RAAS leads to inappropriate retention of sodium and water by the kidneys, increasing blood volume, alongside potent vasoconstriction mediated by angiotensin II. Over time, sustained high pressure causes structural changes in the blood vessel walls, characterized by smooth muscle hypertrophy and lumen narrowing, which further perpetuates the hypertensive state. According to standard clinical guidelines, normal blood pressure is defined as a systolic reading below 120 mmHg and a diastolic reading below 80 mmHg. Elevated blood pressure ranges from 120-129 systolic and less than 80 diastolic. Stage 1 hypertension ranges from 130-139 systolic or 80-89 diastolic, while Stage 2 hypertension involves a systolic reading of 140 mmHg or higher, or a diastolic reading of 90 mmHg or higher. Understanding these physiological ranges and mechanisms enables nursing students to correlate patient clinical presentations with underlying hemodynamic alterations.

headings.title: Classification and Risk Factors of Hypertension
headings.content: Hypertension is broadly classified into two main types: primary (essential) hypertension, which has no identifiable secondary cause and accounts for about 90 to 95 percent of all cases, and secondary hypertension, which is caused by an underlying medical condition such as chronic kidney disease, renal artery stenosis, primary aldosteronism, or endocrine disorders like Cushing's syndrome. Identifying secondary causes is crucial because treating the root pathology can sometimes cure the hypertension. Risk factors for developing hypertension are categorized into non-modifiable and modifiable factors. Non-modifiable risk factors include advancing age, a family history of hypertension, genetic predisposition, and ethnicity, as individuals of African descent frequently experience higher prevalence and more severe complications. Modifiable risk factors are largely lifestyle-driven and include unhealthy dietary habits such as high sodium intake, excessive alcohol consumption, physical inactivity, obesity, chronic psychological stress, and cigarette smoking. For nursing students in Nigeria, recognizing these risk factors in community assessments allows for targeted health education and early intervention strategies, helping to mitigate the rising burden of non-communicable diseases in the region.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Symptoms
headings.content: Hypertension is widely recognized as the 'silent killer' because many affected individuals experience no symptoms at all for years, even when their blood pressure is dangerously high. When symptoms do occur, they are often non-specific and may be attributed to other common ailments. Typical early signs reported by patients include early morning occipital headaches, dizziness, palpitations, fatigue, and sometimes blurred vision due to retinal vessel changes. As the disease progresses and causes target organ damage, symptoms become more pronounced and reflect the specific organ system involved. For instance, cardiac involvement may manifest as dyspnea on exertion, chest pain, or signs of heart failure. Cerebral involvement can lead to transient ischemic attacks or acute stroke symptoms such as unilateral weakness and speech difficulties. Renal impairment may present as nocturia, oliguria, or generalized edema. For nursing students, it is imperative to understand that the absence of symptoms does not equate to the absence of disease. Regular clinical assessment and active screening are necessary to catch hypertension before catastrophic target organ damage develops, ensuring timely interventions in clinical practice.

headings.title: Screening and Assessment in Primary Health Care
headings.content: Screening and assessment in primary health care settings serve as the cornerstone of hypertension control and management. Nurses working in Nigerian primary health care clinics must incorporate routine blood pressure measurement into every patient encounter, regardless of the primary reason for the visit. Proper technique is paramount for accurate diagnosis: the patient should be seated quietly for at least five minutes with feet flat on the floor and arm supported at heart level. The correct cuff size must be used—a cuff that is too small yields falsely high readings, while one that is too large yields falsely low readings. Assessment should also include a comprehensive nursing history, capturing family history, lifestyle habits, current medications, and symptoms of target organ damage. Diagnostic tests often ordered alongside physical assessment include urinalysis to check for protein or blood, fasting blood glucose and lipid profile tests to evaluate cardiovascular risk, and an electrocardiogram (ECG) to assess for left ventricular hypertrophy. Thorough documentation and accurate classification of readings empower the healthcare team to formulate effective, individualized care plans and determine whether referral to a physician or specialist clinic is necessary.

headings.title: Non-Pharmacological Management and Lifestyle Modification
headings.content: Non-pharmacological management and lifestyle modification are foundational components of hypertension therapy, recommended for all patients regardless of whether pharmacological treatment is initiated. Nurses play an educational and motivational role in helping patients adopt and sustain these healthy lifestyle changes. Dietary modifications are paramount, notably the adoption of the Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) eating plan, which emphasizes fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy products while reducing saturated fats and cholesterol. Sodium restriction is critical; patients should be advised to limit salt intake, avoid processed and canned foods heavily seasoned with local bouillon cubes, and utilize alternative herbs and spices for flavoring. Regular aerobic physical activity, such as brisk walking for at least 30 minutes most days of the week, helps reduce vascular resistance and lower blood pressure. Weight management is equally important, as achieving and maintaining a healthy body mass index (BMI) significantly reduces cardiac workload. Additionally, moderation or cessation of alcohol intake, smoking cessation, and effective stress management techniques are vital. For Nigerian patients, lifestyle counseling must be culturally sensitive, practical, and tailored to locally available food items and resources to ensure high compliance.

headings.title: Pharmacological Treatment and Nursing Care
headings.content: When lifestyle modifications are insufficient to achieve target blood pressure goals, pharmacological treatment becomes necessary. Antihypertensive medications are categorized into several major classes, including diuretics (such as thiazides like bendroflumethiazide), beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers (CCBs like amlodipine), angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors (like enalapril), and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs). In many cases, combination therapy is required to achieve control. Nursing care involves close monitoring of blood pressure responses, assessing for potential adverse effects, and promoting strict medication adherence. For instance, nurses must monitor patients on diuretics for electrolyte imbalances such as hypokalemia, watch for dry persistent cough in patients taking ACE inhibitors, and educate patients on CCBs about potential pedal edema and dizziness. Nursing education must emphasize that hypertension is a chronic condition requiring lifelong medication adherence; patients must never stop taking their drugs abruptly when their blood pressure normalizes, as this can trigger dangerous rebound hypertension. Nurses also assess for orthostatic hypotension by measuring blood pressure in lying, sitting, and standing positions, ensuring patient safety against falls in clinical and home environments.

headings.title: Complications and Emergency Management
headings.content: Uncontrolled chronic hypertension can lead to severe, life-threatening complications affecting multiple target organs, most notably the heart, brain, kidneys, and eyes. Cardiac complications include left ventricular hypertrophy, myocardial infarction, and heart failure. Neurological complications involve cerebrovascular accidents (strokes), both ischemic and hemorrhagic, as well as hypertensive encephalopathy. Renal complications culminate in nephrosclerosis and chronic kidney disease, potentially progressing to end-stage renal disease requiring dialysis. Ocular complications, known as hypertensive retinopathy, can cause progressive vision loss. A critical medical emergency associated with this condition is a hypertensive crisis, which is subdivided into hypertensive urgency and hypertensive emergency. A hypertensive emergency occurs when severely elevated blood pressure (typically systolic > 180 mmHg and/or diastolic > 120 mmHg) is accompanied by acute or ongoing damage to target organs. This is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate admission to an intensive care unit, rapid administration of intravenous antihypertensive agents, and continuous arterial blood pressure monitoring. Nursing responsibilities during a hypertensive crisis include maintaining a patent airway, monitoring neurological status, tracking strict fluid intake and output, and administering emergency medications precisely as prescribed.

headings.title: Community Health Education and Prevention Strategies
headings.content: Community health education and primary prevention strategies are essential for reducing the overall incidence and impact of hypertension in Nigeria. Public health nurses play a pivotal role in organizing outreach programs, health talks, and screening camps in churches, mosques, markets, and village squares. These educational campaigns focus on raising awareness about the dangers of high blood pressure, promoting healthy dietary choices such as reducing salt intake, encouraging regular physical activity, and discouraging tobacco use and excessive alcohol consumption. Prevention strategies also involve empowering community members to know their numbers by seeking regular blood pressure checks. Furthermore, community health nurses collaborate with local leaders and policymakers to advocate for supportive environments, such as creating community spaces for walking and promoting access to affordable, nutritious foods. Education must also address cultural myths surrounding hypertension, such as the belief that it can be cured permanently with short herbal courses or that it only affects older or wealthy individuals. By fostering health literacy and active community participation, nurses help bridge the healthcare gap and build a healthier population resilient against cardiovascular diseases.
